Adult females of Cope (Rhinella diptycha) attain a maximum snout-vent length of 19.60 centimeters [Li = 19.60 centimeters], a size notably larger than that achieved by males, whose ultimate SVL reaches 17.13 centimeters [Li = 17.13 centimeters]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism is a common pattern among bufonids and is often linked to fecundity selection, as larger females can accommodate larger clutch volumes. The mass of an individual at the time of hatching is exceedingly low, reflecting the small diameter of the yolk-laden egg. Newly emerged aquatic larvae weigh approximately 0.0018 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0018 grams], a value consistent with the minimal initial investment typical of species that produce large numbers of offspring. This neonatal mass is derived from an egg diameter of about 1.5 millimeters, a dimension that places the species within the typical range for the genus.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the maximum reproductive output of this species is considerable. Females achieve a high fecundity, producing approximately 318 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 318 eggs per clutch] and depositing, on average, one clutch per day [F_R_i = one clutch per day] during peak reproductive bouts. This high daily reproductive rate is a striking feature of Cope, reflecting the strong selective pressures associated with unpredictable, ephemeral breeding ponds in its natural semi-arid habitat. The combined output from such sustained breeding activity underscores the species capacity for rapid population turnover in favorable years. These values were derived from comparative analyses with the congeneric species Rhinella arenarum, adjusted for the larger ultimate body size of Cope.

The transition from an aquatic larval existence to a terrestrial juvenile is marked by metamorphosis, a critical developmental bottleneck. At this transformative stage, the total length of the organism is approximately 3.7 centimeters , a value that provides a baseline for the onset of the post-metamorphic growth phase. Following metamorphosis, the juvenile experiences a period of rapid somatic growth before reaching the threshold for gonadal activation. The snout-vent length at which puberty is attained, signaling the capacity for gametogenesis, is 16.76 centimeters [Lp = 16.76 centimeters]. This size at maturity represents a substantial proportion of the ultimate body length, a pattern that indicates a delayed onset of reproduction in favor of continued body growth, a life-history strategy that is common among large-bodied anurans.

Regarding the ultimate wet weight, a clear divergence emerges between the sexes that mirrors the disparity in length. Females, with their larger skeletal frame, attain a maximum recorded body mass of 837 grams [Wwi = 837 grams], whereas males reach a markedly lower asymptotic mass of 559 grams [Wwi = 559 grams]. This difference of nearly 300 grams underscores the substantial energetic investment females make in egg production and underscores the degree of reproductive allocation required for this species. The attainment of sexual maturity does not immediate guarantee reproductive activity; rather, under the standard thermal regime of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the time since birth at which puberty is completed is approximately 365 days [tp = approximately 365 days]. This one-year timeframe is typical for a bufonid of this body size and aligns with the onset of the first breeding season following the juvenile growth phase.

Longevity in Cope is relatively extended for a medium-to-large bufonid. Under laboratory conditions at a constant 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the documented lifespan reaches approximately 1825 days [am = approximately 1825 days]. This five-year lifespan, while modest compared to some long-lived ranids, is a substantial duration that allows for multiple breeding seasons. The prodigious fecundity of 318 eggs per clutch is finely tuned to the species' reproductive ecology, balancing high investment in gametes against high mortality rates during the early larval stages, ensuring that only a small fraction of the total offspring survive to metamorphosis. The overarching life-history pattern of Cope is thus one of rapid early growth, a substantial delay in maturation until a large body size is achieved, and a sustained, high-effort reproductive strategy over a multi-year adult lifespan under stable thermal conditions.
